elements.quote: High rates of maternal mortality and morbidity remain significant health issues in low- and middle-income countries. Despite this, few researchers have investigated the underlying factors of severe maternal complications in sub-Saharan Africa.
elements.reason: The Background describes the current state of knowledge (high maternal mortality/morbidity in LMICs) and the key uncertainty (few studies of underlying factors of severe maternal complications in sub-Saharan Africa).

elements.quote: Therefore, the objective of this systematic review was to determine the socioeconomic, demographic, and obstetric predictors of severe maternal complications in this region.
elements.reason: The rationale and need for the review are explained: because few researchers have investigated these factors, the review was conducted to determine the predictors of severe maternal complications.

No evidence in the retrieved text indicates that similar systematic reviews exist; the Background presents the review as addressing a gap ('few researchers have investigated'), so no update/replication justification is required.
This is a review of determinants of maternal near miss, not a review of intervention effects, so no mechanism of action needs to be described.
The review examines determinants/associations rather than evaluating a complex intervention, so a logic model of intervention components is not applicable.

elements.quote: The aim of this systematic review was to identify socio-economic, demographic and obstetric factors predictive of maternal near-miss (MNM)in women aged 15-49 years in Africa.
elements.reason: The objective is explicitly stated in the Objectives section, restated in the Background (text_3), and framed as a review question (text_9). A relevant question-formulation framework (PECO) is explicitly applied in text_10, defining Population, Exposure, Comparison, and Outcome.

elements.quote: This review used the PECO (Population, Exposure, Comparison and Outcomes) approach to research
elements.reason: This is a review of determinants/predictors of maternal near-miss, not a review of intervention effects, so PICO-based planned comparisons do not apply; the authors appropriately used PECO instead.

elements.quote: This review used the PECO (Population, Exposure, Comparison and Outcomes) approach to research, with the following parameters: Population: Pregnant, labouring, or postpartum women up to 42 days after delivery in Africa... no prior restrictions on study design (qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods).
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria specify population, exposure, comparison, outcome, setting (Africa), and study designs.
